_comment: data_video1 fixed-camera scene. SOURCE PIXEL coordinates, normalized=false.
LANES ARE NOW DIRECTIONAL. The previous 4 lanes all carried direction
[1.0, 0.11] but spanned y~225-1105, which physically contains BOTH
streams of a two-way road, so 82.8/70.6/42.7/8.9 percent of moving tracks
in lanes 0/1/2/3 opposed that direction.
Evidence (scripts/flow_map_2d.py, scripts/measure_stream_bands.py over all
10200 frames, turning traffic excluded by requiring |vx| > 0.8|vy| and
>= 150 px of travel over 4 s): the main carriageway is a pair of PARALLEL
diagonal bands. Measured percentiles, westbound p05..p95 then eastbound
Least-squares fits used for the lane edges (y = a + b*x):
W far edge  40 + 0.280x     W mid 85.5 + 0.331x     W near edge 131 + 0.382x
E far edge 171 + 0.382x     E mid 305.5 + 0.456x    E near edge 440 + 0.530x
The bands are separated by a constant 40 px median gap so lane_for_point is
unambiguous; the two direction vectors are the measured band slopes, i.e.
(-1, -0.30) for the far/westbound carriageway and (1, +0.47) for the
near/eastbound carriageway.
LANE EXTENTS ARE DELIBERATELY CLIPPED. East of x=2600 the layout is a
junction: a one-way westbound leg (y 720-1200, ~100 percent westbound), a
one-way eastbound leg (y 1200-1920, ~100 percent eastbound) and the lower
two-way road (westbound x<2000 at y 1680-2160). Directional reasoning is
only asserted where the two streams were measured to be cleanly separated,
so the eastbound lanes end at x=2600 and the westbound band narrows after
x=2600 to follow the measured 356 -> 270 -> 208 px width. Everything else
is road_polygons only and therefore carries no direction claim.
Stop line, solid lines, crossings, road_polygons and signal ROIs are
UNCHANGED from the earlier calibration: they were verified independently
and stopped_vehicle queue suppression depends on them. See camera.md.
_reference_note: Coordinates below are pixels in the 3840x2160 authoring resolution.
reference_size lets one authored scene serve every resolution of this
camera: load_scene_config maps them onto the actual video frame, so the
same intersection at 1920x1080 is handled without a second scene file.
_stop_line_note: b_eastbound_stop is the ONLY signal-controlled approach at this camera.
DERIVED, NOT AUTHORED BY EYE. scripts/fit_stop_line_sweep.py places it:
1. The head that governs this line is found by declared approach direction
(SceneContext.signal_for_line), not by image position, because a signal
head is mounted high and projects above the road point it controls.
2. The crossing that head faces is the one traffic queues for. On this
camera that is crossing[1] (centre 1040,276 at 1080p, 161px from the
head) and NOT crossing[0] (207px away). An earlier calibration anchored
to crossing[0] and therefore placed the line inside the junction, where
it was crossed by ordinary through traffic.
3. The line is then swept upstream from that crossing and scored against
the queue itself: the vehicles that HELD the queue (those that stopped
upstream of the crossing, not the ones blocked inside it) are the
calibration target. Setback 80px puts them at -19px and -17px, i.e.
their noses park right at the line; every other setback is worse.
4. The segment is extended perpendicular to travel until it leaves the
governed carriageway on both sides, so it spans the whole approach.
scripts/check_line_span.py asserts this and runs in the test suite.
The old segment covered only the top ~20% of the carriageway, so crossings
on the rest of it were invisible and red_light could not fire at all.
Crossing detection uses the vehicle FRONT bumper (the bbox edge furthest
along `direction`), matching the official definition that the event starts
when the front of the vehicle crosses the line. `direction` is the
measured eastbound travel direction, which is also what queue suppression
needs to decide which side is the approach.
_signal_note: Each signal ROI declares the approach direction it faces. A head is
matched to a stop line by comparing declared directions, NOT by image
position: a head sits several metres up, so its ROI projects well above
the road point it governs and can look 'upstream' in the image. See
signal_eastbound governs the only signal-controlled approach here.
signal_left faces the opposite way and is never used to judge that
line; it would be used only if a westbound stop line were calibrated.
There is no readable signal on the east leg: those heads face away from
this camera, so that region deliberately has no stop line.
